description: Check that DBHost is the endpoint of a DB instance with the FIS-Ready=True tag and take the DB instance's load test lock, so that only one load test runs against it at a time, then run a MySQL load test against it for up to Duration seconds, or until stopped, and report the RDS CPU utilization against TargetCPU

DBHost.description: Endpoint of the DB instance to load. It must be the endpoint of a DB instance in this account and Region that has the FIS-Ready=True tag: the document checks both before it reads the password or connects

DBUsername.description: Database username. The user needs CREATE on the database DBName and on the database fis_loadtest, INSERT and SELECT on DBName's loadtest table, and INSERT, UPDATE and SELECT on fis_loadtest.loadtest_lock

DBPassword.description: Database password. Leave empty (recommended) to read it on the instance from the Secrets Manager secret in DBSecretId. A value here is stored in the experiment template, the experiment, the experiment log, the command parameters and the command script on the instance, and must not contain double quotes, $, `, \ or line breaks.

DBSecretId.description: Name or ARN of the Secrets Manager secret that holds the database password, used when DBPassword is empty: a JSON secret with a password key (for example an RDS-managed secret) or a plain string. The instance role needs secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on it.

Duration.description: Load test duration in seconds, 1 to 780, so that setup (up to 150 seconds), the load, its last status report (up to 45 seconds), the failover check (up to 25 seconds) and the release of the load test lock (up to 20 seconds) finish within the load step's 1020-second timeout. A failover of the DB instance must start and complete while the load runs, and a query must succeed after it, or the document fails. In the experiment template keep RunLoadTest's duration longer than this document can run (120 + 1020 seconds, 19 minutes), so that the document ends while RunLoadTest runs and stopping the experiment cancels the load. With the experiment template's 5-minute wait before the failover, use at least 540 seconds: the wait must end at least 240 seconds before the load does

TargetCPU.description: CPU utilization percentage (0 to 100) to report when reached. It does not decide when the failover starts: the experiment template does

DBInstanceId.description: Identifier of the DB instance whose endpoint DBHost is. Leave empty to use the first part of DBHost

runCommand: # On Amazon Linux 2023, install whichever of the MySQL client, bc and jq are missing. On other operating systems they
# must be installed before the experiment. The step then stops if any tool the document needs is missing: a MySQL
# client, bc, jq, the AWS CLI or GNU timeout.
for c in mysql bc jq aws; do
echo "Missing:$missing. On operating systems other than Amazon Linux 2023, install a MySQL client, bc, jq, the AWS CLI and GNU coreutils before you run the experiment."
echo "Could not find the Region: neither AWS_SSM_REGION_NAME, which SSM Agent sets, nor AWS_DEFAULT_REGION is set."
# If DB_INSTANCE_ID is not provided, try to extract it from the hostname
echo "DB Instance ID not provided, extracted from hostname: $DB_INSTANCE_ID"
# Load only a DB instance the experiment may fault. Before the password is read or any connection is made, check
# that DBHost is the endpoint of DB instance DB_INSTANCE_ID in this account and Region, and that the DB instance has
# the FIS-Ready=True tag. Any error, including a denied or timed-out DescribeDBInstances, stops the test.
echo "Set DBHost to the endpoint of the DB instance to load."
if ! DB_DESC=$(timeout --foreground -k 5 20 aws rds describe-db-instances --region "$REGION" --db-instance-identifier "$DB_INSTANCE_ID" --output json); then
echo "Could not describe DB instance $DB_INSTANCE_ID within 20 seconds. It must exist in this account and Region, and the instance role needs rds:DescribeDBInstances."
echo "DBHost $DB_HOST is not the endpoint of DB instance $DB_INSTANCE_ID (${DB_ENDPOINT:-none}). Stopping without connecting."
echo "DB instance $DB_INSTANCE_ID does not have the FIS-Ready=True tag. Stopping without connecting."
# From here on, use the identifier as RDS stores it, whatever the case of DBHost or DBInstanceId.
echo "DBHost is the endpoint of DB instance $DB_INSTANCE_ID, which has the FIS-Ready=True tag."
# Read the password on the instance when DBPassword is empty, so it is not in the experiment template, the experiment
if ! SECRET=$(timeout --foreground -k 5 20 aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --region "$REGION" --secret-id "$DB_SECRET_ID" --query SecretString --output text); then
echo "Could not read secret $DB_SECRET_ID within 20 seconds. The instance role needs secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on it, and the instance needs a route to Secrets Manager."
echo "Secret $DB_SECRET_ID is JSON but has no password key."
# Credentials go in a client option file, not on the mysql command line. The file is created in memory (/dev/shm),
# opened on descriptor 9 and deleted before anything is written to it, and every mysql call reads it through
# /dev/fd/9, which the workers and their clients inherit. No credentials file is left behind however the script
# ends: a cancelled command is killed with SIGKILL, so no trap would run. The password is escaped for a quoted
# option value (backslash, double quote, line breaks). connect-timeout and the timeout wrapper on every call keep a
# client from hanging on a primary that went away in the failover, so the workers reconnect to the new primary.
# local-infile=0 keeps the server from reading files on the instance through LOAD DATA LOCAL.
# Function to execute SQL and return result
# Function to get the newest CPU utilization datapoint (empty if CloudWatch cannot be read)
# Check connection (without a default database, which may not exist yet)
echo "Failed to connect to MySQL. Please check your connection parameters."
# Create test database and table if they don't exist. Creating the database may be denied when it already exists
# and the user has no CREATE privilege on it, so only a failure to create or use the table stops the test, before
# the failover can hit an idle database.
echo "Setting up test database and tables..."
if ! timeout --foreground -k 5 15 mysql --defaults-extra-file="$CNF" -e "CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS \`$DB_NAME\`;"; then
echo "Could not create database $DB_NAME; continuing in case it already exists."
if ! execute_sql "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS loadtest (
echo "Could not create or use table loadtest in database $DB_NAME. The user needs CREATE, INSERT and SELECT on it."
# Check that the user can insert and read rows before the load starts, so a load that can't run fails here, before
# the failover, instead of running on nothing. This adds one row. The check also reads the largest id in the table:
# the load's queries read only the rows with a larger id, the rows inserted after it, so the rows that earlier runs
# left in the table don't make the load heavier. Autocommit is turned on first, as for the lock, so the row commits.
if ! BASE_ID=$(execute_sql_return "SET autocommit=1; INSERT INTO loadtest (data) VALUES ('setup check'); SELECT MAX(id) FROM loadtest;"); then
echo "Could not insert into and read table loadtest in database $DB_NAME. The user needs INSERT and SELECT on it."
echo "Could not read the largest id in table loadtest in database $DB_NAME: the check returned ${BASE_ID:-nothing}."
# Run only one load test at a time against a DB instance. A second run, from this or another load generator and with
# any DBName, would add its load and connections to this one's, and on a small DB instance class that exhausts the
# connections and the memory. The lock is one row in table loadtest_lock of database fis_loadtest, which the document
# creates if needed. A row survives a failover, which a session's GET_LOCK would not. This run takes the row only if
# its expiry has passed, and holds it until Duration plus 180 seconds from now on the DB instance's clock (UTC). Both
# lock calls turn autocommit on first, so each change commits at once even where the DB instance starts sessions
# with autocommit off (for example through init_connect); the server would otherwise roll the row back when the
# client disconnects. The release is set up before the take, so that a take that commits and then fails is released
# too, and it runs on every exit except a cancel: a cancelled run is killed with SIGKILL, so its row expires on its
# own. A run that can't release the lock says until when it may be held, and fails. A refused run releases nothing.
# A take that fails or times out may still be completed by the DB instance after the release has run, so a run
# whose take failed and that finds no row of its own to release says until when the lock may be held. The clear
# command it prints turns autocommit on too, so that it works in every session.
LOCK_CLEAR="SET autocommit=1; UPDATE fis_loadtest.loadtest_lock SET expires = UTC_TIMESTAMP() - INTERVAL 1 SECOND WHERE id = 1;"

RELEASE_ROW=$(timeout --foreground -k 5 15 mysql --defaults-extra-file="$CNF" --skip-column-names --batch -e "SET autocommit=1; UPDATE fis_loadtest.loadtest_lock SET expires = UTC_TIMESTAMP() - INTERVAL 1 SECOND WHERE id = 1 AND owner = '$LOCK_OWNER'; SELECT owner = '$LOCK_OWNER', expires < UTC_TIMESTAMP() FROM fis_loadtest.loadtest_lock WHERE id = 1;")
echo "Released the load test lock on DB instance $DB_INSTANCE_ID."

echo "The load test lock on DB instance $DB_INSTANCE_ID was no longer this run's when it ended: another load test took it after the lock was cleared or expired, or the lock's row was removed, while this run held it, so another load may have run at the same time."

echo "Could not release the load test lock on DB instance $DB_INSTANCE_ID. Other load tests against the DB instance stop at setup until it expires at $LOCK_EXPIRES UTC. If none runs against it, clear it sooner with: $LOCK_CLEAR"

echo "If the DB instance still completes this run's take of the lock, it holds the lock until $LOCK_HOLD seconds after it completes it, no earlier than about $LOCK_UNTIL UTC, and other load tests against it stop at setup until then. If none runs against it, clear it with: $LOCK_CLEAR"

LOCK_ROW=$(timeout --foreground -k 5 15 mysql --defaults-extra-file="$CNF" --skip-column-names --batch -e "SET autocommit=1; CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS fis_loadtest; CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS fis_loadtest.loadtest_lock (id TINYINT PRIMARY KEY, owner VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, expires DATETIME NOT NULL); INSERT IGNORE INTO fis_loadtest.loadtest_lock (id, owner, expires) VALUES (1, '', '2000-01-01 00:00:00'); UPDATE fis_loadtest.loadtest_lock SET owner = '$LOCK_OWNER', expires = UTC_TIMESTAMP() + INTERVAL $LOCK_HOLD SECOND WHERE id = 1 AND expires < UTC_TIMESTAMP(); SELECT owner, expires FROM fis_loadtest.loadtest_lock WHERE id = 1;")
echo "Could not create or take the load test lock in fis_loadtest.loadtest_lock: the call did not finish within 15 seconds."

echo "Could not create or take the load test lock in fis_loadtest.loadtest_lock. If the error above is an access-denied error, the user needs CREATE on the database fis_loadtest, and INSERT, UPDATE and SELECT on that table."

echo "Another load test (${LOCK_HOLDER:-unknown}) holds the lock on DB instance $DB_INSTANCE_ID until ${HOLDER_EXPIRES:-unknown} UTC, so this run stops before adding a second load. If no other load test runs against this DB instance, clear the lock with: $LOCK_CLEAR"
echo "Took the load test lock on DB instance $DB_INSTANCE_ID until $LOCK_EXPIRES UTC."
# Every query that succeeds appends one byte to an in-memory file that is opened on descriptor 8 and deleted at
# once, as the option file is, so the document counts the load's successful queries without leaving a file behind.
# The file's size is the number of queries that succeeded, and its modification time is when the last one did.
# Each worker is a bash process whose $0 is mysql_load_worker, so `pgrep -af mysql_load_worker` finds the
# workers. This script counts and stops only its own background jobs (jobs -pr), never processes found by name
# or by a saved PID that may have been reused, so two runs on one load generator don't stop each other's load. A
# query already running ends on its own within its timeout. Each query that succeeds appends a byte to descriptor 8.
# Each SELECT reads only the rows with an id larger than BASE_ID, the rows inserted after the setup.
# Arguments: end time, worker id, database, BASE_ID.
# Insert random data. Autocommit is turned on first, as for the lock, so the row commits and the queries read it
timeout --foreground -k 5 15 mysql --defaults-extra-file="$CNF" "$db" -e "SET autocommit=1; INSERT INTO loadtest (data) VALUES (REPEAT(MD5(RAND()), 8));" && printf . >&8
# Run complex queries to increase CPU load
timeout --foreground -k 5 15 mysql --defaults-extra-file="$CNF" "$db" -e "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loadtest WHERE id > $base_id AND id % 10 = $worker_id;" && printf . >&8
timeout --foreground -k 5 15 mysql --defaults-extra-file="$CNF" "$db" -e "SELECT AVG(LENGTH(data)) FROM loadtest WHERE id > $base_id AND id % 10 = $worker_id;" && printf . >&8
timeout --foreground -k 5 15 mysql --defaults-extra-file="$CNF" "$db" -e "SELECT data, COUNT(*) FROM loadtest WHERE id > $base_id GROUP BY data HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 LIMIT 10;" && printf . >&8
# Run a join query that scans the rows the load inserted

timeout --foreground -k 5 15 mysql --defaults-extra-file="$CNF" "$db" -e "SELECT a.id, b.id, LENGTH(a.data) + LENGTH(b.data) FROM loadtest a JOIN loadtest b ON a.id % 100 = b.id % 100 WHERE a.id > $base_id AND b.id > $base_id LIMIT 100;" && printf . >&8
# Start worker processes in background; their query output is discarded
echo "Starting $CONCURRENCY worker processes for up to $MAX_DURATION seconds..."
echo "Their queries read only the rows with an id larger than $BASE_ID."
# Report every 30 seconds while the load runs. The experiment template, not this script, decides when the failover
# starts, so reaching TargetCPU is only reported. The test fails, because the load isn't running, if no query has
# succeeded 60 seconds after the workers started, if no query has succeeded for more than 180 seconds after that,
# longer than the 60 to 120 seconds a failover typically takes, or if all workers stop before the end time.
echo "Load running. Reporting every 30 seconds the queries that succeeded and the CPU utilization (target $TARGET_CPU%)..."
echo "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S'): all workers have stopped before the end of the load. Something else stopped them, so the load was cut short."
echo "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S'): no query has succeeded 60 seconds after the workers started, so the load isn't running. Stopping the workers."
echo "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S'): no query has succeeded for more than 180 seconds, so the load stopped. Stopping the workers."
CONNECTIONS=$(execute_sql_return "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.processlist WHERE user = '$DB_USER';" 2>/dev/null)
cpu_text="not available (could not read the metric; the instance role needs cloudwatch:GetMetricStatistics)"
echo "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S'): workers running: $alive, queries succeeded since the last report: $((ok - reported)), active connections: ${CONNECTIONS:-unknown}, CPU utilization: $cpu_text"
# Stop any of this script's workers still in their last loop, so the load ends at Duration even when queries are
# slow, then wait for them. A query already running ends on its own within its timeout.
echo "No query succeeded during the load, so the load didn't run."
echo "No query succeeded in the last 30 seconds of the load, so the load stopped before its end."
# The experiment fails the DB instance over while the load runs. Read this DB instance's failover events from the
# start to the end of the load, and fail unless a failover started and completed in that time and a query succeeded
# after it completed. Otherwise the failover wasn't under load: for example the install and setup took longer than
# the wait before the failover, the load ended before the failover completed, or the load had stopped.

if ! EVENTS=$(timeout --foreground -k 5 20 aws rds describe-events --region "$REGION" --source-type db-instance --source-identifier "$DB_INSTANCE_ID" --event-categories failover --start-time "$LOAD_START_ISO" --end-time "$END_ISO" --output json); then
echo "Could not read the RDS events of DB instance $DB_INSTANCE_ID within 20 seconds. The instance role needs rds:DescribeEvents."
FAILOVER_STARTED=$(printf '%s' "$EVENTS" | jq -r '[.Events[]? | select(.Message | test("failover.*started"; "i"))] | first | .Date // empty')
echo "No failover of DB instance $DB_INSTANCE_ID started while the load ran, from $LOAD_START_ISO to $END_ISO, so the failover was not under load."
FAILOVER_DONE=$(printf '%s' "$EVENTS" | jq -r --arg s "$FAILOVER_STARTED" '[.Events[]? | select(.Date >= $s and (.Message | test("failover.*complete"; "i")))] | first | .Date // empty')
echo "The failover of DB instance $DB_INSTANCE_ID that started at $FAILOVER_STARTED did not complete before the load ended at $END_ISO, so the load did not run on the new primary."
echo "Could not read the time $FAILOVER_DONE of the failover's completion event of DB instance $DB_INSTANCE_ID."
echo "No query succeeded after the failover of DB instance $DB_INSTANCE_ID completed at $FAILOVER_DONE, so the load did not run on the new primary."
ABANDONED=$(printf '%s' "$EVENTS" | jq -r '[.Events[]? | select(.Message | test("abandoning.*failover"; "i"))] | first | .Date // empty')

echo "RDS abandoned a requested failover of DB instance $DB_INSTANCE_ID at $ABANDONED because a failover had recently occurred, so the failover in this run's window may not have been the experiment's own."
echo "A failover of DB instance $DB_INSTANCE_ID started at $FAILOVER_STARTED and completed at $FAILOVER_DONE, while the load ran."
echo "Load test finished (target CPU reached: $target_reached). Queries that succeeded: $total."
